newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Talks on North project positive - council.
newsitem.headline: Talks on North project positive - council.

text.p: A meeting between North Ltd and environmentalists over the stalled Lake Cowal gold mine project had led to a narrowing of differences, the New South Wales Labor Council said on Thursday.
Peter Sams, secretary of the Labor Council, which chaired the meeting, said there were legitimate environmental concerns about the A$220 million project.

The New South Wales state Labor government in April 1996 refused a development application for the mine on environmental grounds linked to the discharge of cyanide after North had already spent some A$26 million on the project.
"We are narrowing those (environmental) differences and discussions will continue," Sams told reporters after receiving a report into the economic impact of the project.

The report, prepared by the independent Centre for International Economics for the local Bland Shire Council, found the project would provide 180 jobs and A$9 million in wages for the depressed region, with up to 300 jobs during construction.
Sams, who is also the state Labor Party president, said it would be a great loss to the community if the project did not proceed.
He said he was heartened by the level of co-operation between the company and environmentalists at Wednesday's meeting, and by the fact that meetings would continue.
Lake Cowal is one of the largest fresh water lakes in New South Wales.
Conservationists believe it is home to some 170 species of birds and needs to be protected.
North has projected the mine would produce 232,000 ounces of gold per year over the first seven years and 100,000 ounces per year over a remaining four-year mine life.
